input:
The Nusselt number is a dimensionless quantity that is widely used in heat transfer, and it can be understood as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. In other words, the comparison is made at one and the same surface and under the same temperature difference: the numerator of the ratio is the heat that is actually carried away from the surface by the moving fluid, while the denominator is the heat that conduction alone would carry across a stagnant layer of the fluid under exactly the same conditions. Because the Nusselt number is a ratio of two heat transfer rates expressed in the same units, it has no units of its own.

A value near 1 means that convection is adding very little to conduction, so the fluid at the surface is transferring heat at roughly the rate that a stagnant layer would transfer it, and the heat transfer at the surface is, in effect, limited by conduction. A large value, on the other hand, means that the motion of the fluid carries heat away much more rapidly than conduction across the layer would do, so the resistance at the surface becomes small in comparison with the conduction reference. Overall, the Nusselt number expresses the strength of surface convection measured against a fixed conduction reference, and comparisons between different cases are always comparisons against that same reference. It should be noted that the number does not by itself state the heat flux, since the flux also depends on the temperature difference and on the conduction reference for the particular geometry being considered.

The Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. The comparison is made at the same surface and under the same temperature difference. The numerator of the ratio is the heat carried away from the surface by the moving fluid; the denominator is the heat that conduction alone would carry across a stagnant layer of the fluid under the same conditions. The Nusselt number is dimensionless, because the two rates in the ratio carry the same units.

A value near 1 means that convection adds little to conduction. The fluid at the surface transfers heat at about the rate a stagnant layer would transfer it, and surface heat transfer is in effect conduction-limited. A large value means the opposite balance: the motion of the fluid carries heat away much faster than conduction across the layer would, and the resistance at the surface is small against the conduction reference.

The Nusselt number states the strength of surface convection against a fixed conduction reference, and a comparison between two cases is a comparison against that same reference. The number does not state the heat flux. The flux depends also on the temperature difference and on the conduction reference for the geometry in question, and two surfaces with the same Nusselt number can carry different fluxes.
